summary: Describes considerations for mailing lists when non-ASCII UTF-8 email addresses are introduced. It outlines possible scenarios for lists that mix non-ASCII and traditional addresses, but does not specify protocol changes or offer implementation or deployment advice. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Some email addresses now contain characters outside plain ASCII, and a mailing list has to handle both kinds of member. This RFC sets out the questions an operator has to answer, describes the two kinds of list that can result, and explains why the bounce address and the list headers need special care. It deliberately stops short of prescribing a solution.

questions: mailing lists with internationalized email addresses
utf-8 email addresses on mailing lists
mixing ascii and non-ascii list members
how do mailing lists downgrade headers
how do mailing lists handle non-ascii addresses
subtitle: What a mailing list has to decide when some of its members have email addresses that are not plain ASCII.

tldr.problem: Internationalized email addresses break the assumption that a mailing list can take one message and hand the same message to every subscriber. A list agent has to decide what it can accept, what it can send, and what it does with a sender whose address cannot be written in plain ASCII.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC works through three questions to ask of a list, two kinds of list, fully SMTPUTF8 and mixed, the effect on bounce addresses, and the list headers that have to be built out of ASCII-only URLs.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that lists the possible scenarios and the problems in each. It specifies no protocol changes and gives no implementation or deployment advice.

facts.label: Three capabilities of a list
facts.value: A non-ASCII submission address, non-ASCII subscriptions, and accepting SMTPUTF8 messages

facts.label: List header character set
facts.value: List-* headers permit only ASCII text, including in the URLs

facts.label: ASCII encoding of non-ASCII
facts.value: A pair of hex digits preceded by a percent sign

facts.label: List identifier
facts.value: The List-ID header field uniquely identifies a list and is meant to remain constant

facts.label: Per-recipient bounce addresses
facts.value: Variable Envelope Return Paths, one per recipient or per message per recipient

facts.label: Downgrading rule
facts.value: If a downgraded version of an SMTPUTF8 message is prepared, all the List-* headers must be downgraded

today: RFC 6783 was published in November 2012 as an Informational document and obsoletes RFC 5983, an earlier Experimental document on the same subject. It has not been obsoleted or updated since. The document lists possible scenarios for handling lists that mix non-ASCII and traditional addresses, but it specifies no protocol changes and offers no implementation or deployment advice.

sections.title: What Changes When Addresses Are Not ASCII
sections.content:
The RFC describes considerations for mailing lists with the introduction of non-ASCII UTF-8 email addresses, whose usage is described in RFC 6530. Mailing lists matter because they are an important part of email usage and collaborative communications, and internationalized addresses affect them in three main areas: transport, meaning receiving and sending messages; the message headers of received and retransmitted messages; and mailing list operational policies.

A mailing list is a mechanism that distributes a message to multiple recipients when the originator sends it to a single address. An agent, usually software rather than a person, at that address receives the message and then causes it to be redistributed to a list of recipients. That agent usually sets the envelope return address, the bounce address, of the redistributed message to a different address from that of the original message, so that error and other automatically generated messages go to an address associated with the list rather than to the original sender, who typically does not control the list.

In most cases the list agent redistributes a received message to its subscribers as a new message, conceptually using message submission as the original sender did. The exception, where the list is not managed by a separate agent but by an expansion step inside one SMTP transaction, is not addressed by this document.

While the mail transport protocol is the same for regular recipients and list recipients, list agents have special considerations with non-ASCII addresses because they retransmit messages composed by other agents to potentially many recipients. There are considerations in the envelope as well as in the header fields of redistributed messages, and in particular a message with non-ASCII addresses in the headers or envelope cannot be sent to non-SMTPUTF8 recipients.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the trouble comes from the fact that a list does not simply forward what it receives. It rebuilds the message and sends a new one to every member, and it changes the return address so that delivery failures come back to the list rather than to the sender. Once an address contains characters outside plain ASCII, that rebuilding has to decide what to do with them.

sections.title: Three Questions to Ask About a List
sections.content:
The RFC divides the problem into two kinds of consideration. The first is purely technical, involving message handling and error cases. A list agent that is unprepared to handle SMTPUTF8 mail might simply choose to reject all messages from non-ASCII addresses. The second arises from the fact that humans use mailing lists to communicate. A user who sends a message to a list is often unaware of the list membership, and neither the sender nor the recipients personally know each other, so remedies that would be readily available in one-to-one communication are not appropriate. If a message is undeliverable, a person could normally telephone or use instant messaging to find a working address; on a mailing list the users may have no such recourse, and the original sender usually does not know which members received the message or whether it was undeliverable to some.

Conceptually, the internationalization of a mailing list divides into three capabilities. First, does the list have a non-ASCII submission address? Second, does the list agent accept subscriptions for addresses containing non-ASCII characters? And third, does the list agent accept messages that require SMTPUTF8 capabilities? If a list has subscribers with ASCII addresses, those subscribers might or might not be able to accept SMTPUTF8 messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Three questions decide how hard a list's life is: can people post to it using a non-ASCII address, can people subscribe with one, and will it accept a message that needs the newer transport. A list that answers no to all three behaves exactly as it did before, which is the easy case.

sections.title: Fully SMTPUTF8 Lists and Mixed Lists
sections.content:
Some lists may wish to be fully SMTPUTF8, meaning that all subscribers are expected to be able to receive SMTPUTF8 mail. For list hygiene such a list would probably want to prevent subscriptions from addresses unable to receive SMTPUTF8 mail. If a prospective subscriber has a non-ASCII address, it must be able to receive SMTPUTF8 mail, but there is no way to tell whether a subscriber with an ASCII address can receive SMTPUTF8 mail short of sending an SMTPUTF8 probe or confirmation message and somehow finding out whether it was delivered, for example if the user clicked a link in the confirmation message.

Other lists may wish to handle a mixture of SMTPUTF8 and ASCII subscribers, either as a transitional measure as subscribers upgrade to SMTPUTF8-capable mail software or as an ongoing feature. While it is not possible in general to downgrade SMTPUTF8 mail to ASCII mail, list software might divide the recipients into two sets, SMTPUTF8 and ASCII recipients, and create a downgraded version of the list message to send to the ASCII recipients.

To determine which set an address belongs in, list software might make the conservative assumption that ASCII addresses get ASCII messages, it might try to probe the address with an SMTPUTF8 test message, or it might let the subscriber set the message format manually, similar to the way that some lists let subscribers choose between plain text and HTML mail, or between individual messages and a daily digest. To determine whether a message needs to be downgraded, list software might assume that any message received over an SMTPUTF8 SMTP session is an SMTPUTF8 message, or might examine the headers and body of the message to see whether it needs SMTPUTF8 treatment. Depending on the interface between the list software and the Mail Transfer Agent and Mail Delivery Agent that handle incoming messages, it may not be able to tell the type of session an incoming message arrived on.
sections.plainLanguage: A list that only has modern members can send one message to everybody. A list with a mixture has to sort its members into two groups and send two versions of each message. Working out which group a member belongs in is the hard part, because an ordinary ASCII address gives no clue whether that person can receive a message with non-ASCII characters in it.

sections.title: Bounce Addresses and VERP
sections.content:
Mailing list software usually changes the envelope addresses on each message. The bounce address is set to an address that will return bounces to the list agent, and the recipient addresses are set to the subscribers of the list. For some lists, all messages to a list get the same bounce address. For others, list software may create a bounce address per recipient, or a unique bounce address per message per recipient, techniques known as Variable Envelope Return Paths, or VERP.

The bounce address for a list typically includes the name of the list, so a list with a non-ASCII name will have a non-ASCII bounce address. Given the unknown paths that bounce messages might take, list software might instead use an ASCII bounce address to make it more likely that bounces can be delivered back to the list agent. Similarly, a VERP address for each subscriber typically embeds a version of the subscriber's address, so the VERP bounce address for a non-ASCII subscriber address will itself be a non-ASCII address. For the same reason, the list software might use ASCII bounce addresses that encode the recipient's identity in some other way.
sections.plainLanguage: Delivery failures have to come back to the list, not to the sender. The address they come back to is usually built from the list's own name, and the per-recipient variant used by some lists embeds the subscriber's address. If either of those contains non-ASCII characters, the failure message may not get back, so list software may have to invent an ASCII substitute.

sections.title: List Headers Have to Stay ASCII
sections.content:
List agents typically add list-specific headers to each message before resending it. The headers specified in RFCs 2369 and 2919 were all defined before SMTPUTF8 mail existed, and their definitions do not address where non-ASCII characters might appear. The list headers include List-Id, List-Help, List-Unsubscribe, List-Subscribe, List-Post, List-Owner and List-Archive. RFC 2369 says the contents of the list header fields mostly consist of angle-bracket enclosed URLs with internal whitespace being ignored, and RFC 2919 says the list identifier will in most cases appear like a host name in a domain of the list owner. Because these headers were defined in the context of ASCII mail, they permit only ASCII text, including in the URLs. The most commonly used URI schemes in List-* headers tend to be http and mailto, although they sometimes include https and ftp and in principle can contain any valid URI.

Even if a scheme permits an internationalized form, it should use a pure ASCII form of the URI. Future work may extend these header fields or define replacements to support unencoded non-ASCII, but in the absence of such an extension or replacement, non-ASCII characters can only be included by encoding them as ASCII. The encoding technique is to use a pair of hex digits preceded by a percent sign. Percent signs, however, have been used informally in mail addresses to do source routing, and although few mail systems still permit source routing, a lot of mail software still forbids or escapes the characters formerly used for it, which can lead to unfortunate interactions with percent-encoded URIs.

There is no standard or even informal way for mail user agents to signal SMTPUTF8 capabilities, so a program cannot know whether it may pass a URI in unencoded non-ASCII. The RFC also notes that whether internationalized domain names should be percent-encoded or appear in A-label form depends on the context in which they occur.

The List-ID header field is treated separately because it uniquely identifies a list and is meant to stay constant even if the system operating the list changes. It is often used in filters and tests, such as client-side filters and Sieve filters. If the definition were extended to allow non-ASCII text, filters might not properly compare encoded and unencoded versions of a non-ASCII value. It is also generally desirable that this field contain something meaningful that users can type in, and ASCII encodings of non-ASCII characters are unlikely to be meaningful to users or easy for them to type accurately.
sections.plainLanguage: The headers that tell a mail program about the list, such as where to subscribe and where to get help, were written before non-ASCII addresses existed and only allow plain ASCII. A non-ASCII character therefore has to be written as a percent sign followed by two hex digits, and because old mail programs still treat percent signs specially, that can itself cause trouble. The list's identifier is held to the same rule, because filters compare it.

sections.title: Downgrading a Message and the Sender's Address
sections.content:
If list software prepares a downgraded version of an SMTPUTF8 message, all the List-* headers must be downgraded. In particular, if a List-* header contains a non-ASCII mailto, even encoded in ASCII, it may be advisable to edit the header to remove the non-ASCII address or replace it with an equivalent ASCII address if one is known to the list software, because a client might run into trouble if the decoded mailto results in a non-ASCII address. If a header that contains a mailto URL is downgraded by percent encoding, some mail software may misinterpret the percent signs as attempted source routing.

It may not be possible to produce a downgraded version that is satisfactorily equivalent to the original. If a non-ASCII List-ID is downgraded to an ASCII version, software and humans at recipient systems will typically not be able to tell that both refer to the same list. If lists permit mail with multiple MIME parts, some MIME headers in SMTPUTF8 messages may include non-ASCII characters in file names and other descriptive text strings. Downgrading those strings may lose the sense of the names, break references from other MIME parts, such as HTML image references to embedded images, and otherwise damage the mail.

One case has no good answer. List software typically leaves the original submitter's address in the From line, both so that recipients can tell who wrote the message and so that they have a choice of responding to the list or directly to the submitter. If a submitter has a non-ASCII address, there is no way to downgrade the From header and preserve the address so that ASCII recipients can respond to it, since non-SMTPUTF8 mail systems cannot send mail to non-ASCII addresses. The RFC lists work-arounds, none of which it knows to be implemented: letting subscribers with non-ASCII addresses register an alternate ASCII address with the list software, having the list software create ASCII forwarding addresses itself, or putting the list's own address in the From line and losing the ability to respond directly to the submitter.

The RFC's Security Considerations section says there are none beyond what mailing list agents do now.
sections.plainLanguage: Turning a modern message into an old-style one loses something each time: the list headers may have to lose their non-ASCII addresses, the list's own identifier may become a different-looking string, and file names in attached parts can be mangled. The hardest case is the sender's own address, because there is no old-style way to write it, so replies to the person can no longer reach them.
